title: GBP 1,000 spent on day one of the cycle. No interest for 45 days. Spent on day 29, far less.
explain:
A cardholder spends GBP 1,000 on the first day of the billing cycle.
The statement arrives, and the cardholder pays in full 21 days later.
No interest is charged, and the cardholder assumes every purchase gets 45 days free.

Here is how that happens:

→ GBP 1,000 spent at the start of the cycle
→ Statement sent at cycle end
→ Full payment inside the 21 day window
→ No interest charged this time

The requirement said:
"Every card purchase gets 45 days interest free."

Why?

The interest-free credit period depends on where in the billing cycle the payment fell, and it can reach about 45 days for a payment made at the start of a cycle. When the cycle ends, the issuer sends the statement, and the cardholder then has a set period, usually about 21 days, to pay. Paying the full statement amount inside that window means no interest, while paying less leaves interest charged on the balance.

The free window depends on the day you spend, not the card you hold.

BA Takeaway

State the window as a range tied to the purchase date, never as a single number.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Purchase date in the cycle
→ Statement date
→ Payment window

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves how many interest-free days this purchase actually gets?"

Have you explained the free credit window as a fixed number when it is not?
takeaway: The free window depends on the day you spend, not the card you hold.

parts.label: Free credit up to 45 days
parts.note: A payment at the start of a cycle can stretch to about 45 days.

parts.label: Statement ends the cycle
parts.note: The issuer sends the statement when the cycle ends.

parts.label: About 21 days to pay
parts.note: The cardholder then has usually about 21 days to pay.

parts.label: Pay in full, no interest
parts.note: Full payment inside the window means no interest is charged.

parts.label: Pay less, interest charged
parts.note: Paying less leaves interest charged on the balance.

title: A merchant pays GBP 100 in card fees. GBP 80 of it goes to a bank the customer never sees.
explain:
A merchant accepts a card payment and pays GBP 100 in merchant service charges.
About GBP 80 of that goes to the issuer.
The merchant asks the customer to cover it, and the customer refuses.

Here is how that happens:

→ Card transaction settled
→ Merchant service charges of GBP 100 applied
→ Interchange of about GBP 80 paid to the issuer
→ Merchant tries to pass the cost to the cardholder

The requirement said:
"The cardholder pays the interchange fee."

Why?

Interchange is what the acquirer pays the issuer per card transaction, known too as the wholesale fee or interexchange fee. It is the issuer's transaction fee in clearing and settlement, typically running to 75 to 85 percent of the merchant service charges. The merchant bears this cost through the fees charged on the transaction, not the cardholder.

Interchange is the acquirer paying the issuer. The merchant bears it.

BA Takeaway

Name the payer and the bearer of every card fee in the requirement, so no flow charges the wrong party.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Acquirer payment
→ Issuer receipt
→ Merchant cost

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves who bears this fee?"

Have you seen a fee charged to the wrong side of a card transaction?
takeaway: Interchange is the acquirer paying the issuer. The merchant bears it.

parts.note: Compensation the acquirer pays the issuer per transaction.

parts.label: Also called
parts.note: Wholesale fee or interexchange fee.

parts.label: Size
parts.note: Typically 75 to 85 percent of merchant service charges.

parts.label: Who bears it
parts.note: The merchant bears the cost, not the cardholder.

One thing to remember: Interchange is the acquirer paying the issuer. The merchant bears it.

title: Two merchants, same volume, wildly different scheme bills. The cards were different.
explain:
Two merchants each process the same volume.
One takes mostly one scheme's cards, the other the other scheme's.
Their scheme bills look nothing alike, and neither merchant can explain why.

Here is how that happens:

→ Merchants process the same volume
→ Different card mix on each merchant
→ Scheme fees charged in different ways
→ Bills differ with no explanation

The requirement said:
"Scheme fees are charged the same way by every scheme."

Why?

The card schemes collect fees from merchants alongside the processor, and each scheme charges in its own way. The processing firm usually takes what it is owed straight from the merchant's account. Mastercard charges per transaction, while Visa charges yearly or quarterly memberships, so a merchant's scheme cost depends on which cards its customers use and how much volume goes through each scheme.

Same volume, different scheme bill. The card mix decides it.

BA Takeaway

Break every scheme cost down by scheme and by charging method, so a merchant can see what drives the bill.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Processor fees
→ Per transaction charges
→ Membership charges

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves which scheme drove this merchant's bill?"

Have you compared two merchants' card costs without checking the card mix?
takeaway: Same volume, different scheme bill. The card mix decides it.

parts.label: Processor
parts.note: Usually takes its fees straight from the merchant account.

parts.label: Mastercard
parts.note: Charges per transaction.

parts.label: Visa
parts.note: Charges yearly or quarterly memberships.

parts.label: Merchant cost varies
parts.note: Cost depends on card mix and volume through each scheme.

One thing to remember: Same volume, different scheme bill. The card mix decides it.

title: EUR 100,000 was due to settle. Both banks waited for the other to move it.
explain:
A EUR 100,000 credit transfer sits ready to settle.
Each bank assumes the other will move the funds.
The payment waits, and the beneficiary calls to ask where the money is.

Here is how that happens:

→ pacs.008 ready for EUR 100,000
→ Settlement method field never read
→ Each bank waits for the other
→ Payment stalls with no owner

The requirement said:
"Settlement happens by itself once the instruction is sent."

Why?

In an ISO 20022 credit transfer the settlement method is the field that assigns settlement to one bank in the chain. INDA puts settlement on the instructed agent, so the next bank moves the funds, while INGA puts it on the instructing agent, so the sending bank moves the funds itself. Read the field first in any funding dispute, because it fixes which bank must hold the liquidity, which account is debited, and how both sides reconcile.

INDA or INGA decides who moves the funds. Read it first.

BA Takeaway

Make the settlement method the first field read in every funding dispute, and name the settling bank before anything else is investigated.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Settlement method field
→ Settling bank liquidity
→ Account debited

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves which bank must move these funds?"

Have you watched two banks wait for each other to settle a payment?
takeaway: INDA or INGA decides who moves the funds. Read it first.

parts.label: INDA
parts.note: Instructed agent settles; the next bank moves funds.

parts.label: INGA
parts.note: Instructing agent settles; the sending bank moves funds.

parts.label: Liquidity burden
parts.note: Liquidity must sit with the settling bank.

parts.label: Settlement timing
parts.note: Settlement timing follows the settling bank.

Each bank assumes the other will move the funds. The payment waits, and the beneficiary calls to ask where the money is. One thing to remember: INDA or INGA decides who moves the funds. Read it first.

title: A customer paid INR 50,000 by UPI in seconds. The banks settled hours later.
explain:
A customer pays INR 50,000 by UPI.
The debit shows at once and the merchant confirms receipt in seconds.
The payment then fails in reconciliation, and the team treats it as a customer failure.

Here is how that happens:

→ UPI debit of INR 50,000 at once
→ Merchant receipt confirmed in seconds
→ Interbank settlement still pending
→ Reconciliation failure blamed on the customer leg

The requirement said:
"Instant for the customer means instant for the banks."

Why?

UPI compresses the customer experience into seconds, debit seen at once, merchant receipt confirmed almost immediately, while the banks still settle with each other later under the scheme settlement cycle. Customer leg and interbank settlement are two separate events, and the bank funds the liquidity and reconciliation exposure between them. In any failure, separate the two events first and ask which one broke: the customer leg or the settlement leg.

Instant to the customer, settled later between banks.

BA Takeaway

Separate the customer leg from the settlement leg before diagnosing any UPI failure.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Customer leg
→ Settlement leg
→ Liquidity gap

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves which leg broke, the customer leg or the settlement leg?"

Have you blamed a customer leg for a settlement leg failure?
takeaway: Instant to the customer, settled later between banks.

parts.note: Account debited at once.

parts.label: Credit in seconds
parts.note: Receipt confirmed within seconds.

parts.label: Settlement later
parts.note: Banks settle later, on the scheme cycle.

parts.label: The gap the bank funds
parts.note: The bank funds the gap in between.

title: A EUR 600 collection was rejected. The mandate evidence was in three systems, and none of it matched.
explain:
A EUR 600 collection is rejected for a missing or invalid mandate.
The mandate evidence is scattered: a paper scan in a shared drive, an online consent in another system, an amendment as a free-text note.
The rejection cannot be explained, and the customer is not convinced either.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 600 collection rejected
→ Mandate evidence scattered across systems
→ Amendment recorded as a free-text note
→ Rejection cannot be explained to the customer

The requirement said:
"A mandate is a record you file once."

Why?

Think of a mandate as a lifecycle, created, amended when a customer changes bank accounts, and cancelled, with a reference and evidence at every step. Scatter that evidence, a paper scan in a shared drive, an online consent in another system, an amendment as a free-text note, and a collection rejected for a missing or invalid mandate becomes unexplainable. Give billing one view of each mandate, its current state and the evidence that proves it.

A mandate is a lifecycle, not a record.

BA Takeaway

Hold one view of each mandate, its current state and the evidence at every step, from creation to cancellation.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Mandate creation
→ Mandate amendment
→ Mandate cancellation
→ Mandate evidence

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this mandate is valid, and where does it live?"

Have you tried to defend a collection when the mandate evidence was scattered?
takeaway: A mandate is a lifecycle, not a record.

steps.note: Record the mandate with its reference.

steps.note: Log changes such as a new bank account.

title: A EUR 450 mandate was amended twice. The collections could not be traced to it.
explain:
A EUR 450 mandate is amended when the customer changes bank accounts.
The amendment is recorded under a new reference.
When the collections are challenged, none of them trace back to the mandate that authorised them.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 450 mandate created with one reference
→ Amendment recorded under a new reference
→ Collections challenged by the debtor
→ No collection traces to the authorising mandate

The requirement said:
"A new amendment needs a new mandate reference."

Why?

A mandate reference is generated once and stays with the mandate from creation through amendments to cancellation. Every amendment and cancellation is recorded against it with an audit history, so any collection traces back to the mandate that authorised it. Reuse it, change it or lose it and the mandate cannot be proven, and its collections cannot be defended.

One mandate, one reference, for its whole life.

BA Takeaway

Generate the reference once, record every change against it, and never reuse or change it.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Mandate reference
→ Amendment history
→ Cancellation record
→ Audit trail

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this collection traces to the mandate that authorised it?"

Have you seen a collection fail because its mandate reference had changed?
takeaway: One mandate, one reference, for its whole life.

parts.note: Created once and unique to the mandate.

parts.label: Amendments logged
parts.note: Logged against the same reference.

parts.label: Cancellation logged
parts.note: Logged against the same reference.

parts.note: Each change is traceable.

title: A business was collected under Core. It claimed a refund the creditor never expected.
explain:
A business is collected under SDD Core for EUR 5,000.
The debtor claims a refund the creditor assumed did not exist.
The creditor had run one process for both schemes, and the differences were hidden.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 5,000 collected under Core
→ Debtor claims a refund
→ Creditor assumed no refund right existed
→ One process used for both schemes

The requirement said:
"Core and B2B can run on one process."

Why?

Core and B2B differ exactly where risk is decided: who may use them, what refund rights the debtor holds, and what the debtor bank must verify before the first collection. A business collected under Core holds a refund right the creditor may not expect, while under B2B there is no such right but the mandate must be verified first. Running one process for both hides those differences, so record the scheme on each mandate and follow that scheme's current rulebook.

Two schemes, two risk profiles. One process hides them.

BA Takeaway

Record the scheme on each mandate and follow that scheme's rulebook, never a blended process.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Scheme on the mandate
→ Refund rights
→ Mandate verification

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves which scheme governs this mandate?"

Have you run one process for Core and B2B and been caught by the difference?
takeaway: Two schemes, two risk profiles. One process hides them.

parts.note: Core: consumers and businesses. B2B: businesses only.

parts.label: Debtor refund rights
parts.note: Core debtors hold a refund right; B2B debtors do not.

parts.label: Mandate verification
parts.note: B2B mandates are verified before the first collection.

title: A EUR 140 transfer arrived short by 11.39 percent. The customer was told the fee was small.
explain:
A customer sends EUR 140 abroad.
About 11.39 percent disappears in fees before it arrives.
The customer was quoted one small fee, and nobody split the total into its parts.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 140 transfer sent
→ Total fee of about 11.39 percent taken
→ Fee never split into components
→ Customer cannot compare corridors

The requirement said:
"The fee on a transfer is one charge."

Why?

Take the cited example, a 140 euro transfer carrying an 11.39 percent fee, and the corridor cost structure becomes visible: the fee is not one charge but transfer fee plus exchange margin plus intermediary charges along the route. Splitting the total into components is what lets a customer compare corridors and an analyst say which part is avoidable. These figures describe that cited example only, not every transfer on the corridor, so present them as one case, never as the corridor rate.

One transfer, three stacked charges. Split the total to see them.

BA Takeaway

Split every transfer fee into transfer fee, exchange margin and intermediary charges, and label the example as one case only.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Transfer fee
→ Exchange margin
→ Intermediary charges

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves what each part of this fee actually cost?"

Have you quoted a transfer fee that hid two more charges inside it?
takeaway: One transfer, three stacked charges. Split the total to see them.

parts.note: Charged for sending the payment.

parts.label: FX margin
parts.note: Cost hidden inside the FX rate.

parts.label: Charges en route
parts.note: Taken by banks along the route.

parts.label: Total paid
parts.note: What the customer actually pays in this one example.

title: A EUR 10,000 SDD collection fell on a national holiday abroad. The team moved the due date.
explain:
A EUR 10,000 SDD collection is due on a day that is a national holiday in another country.
The team moves the due date, assuming the holiday stops the collection.
The collection was valid all along, because the interbank leg runs on TARGET.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 10,000 SDD collection due
→ National holiday in another country
→ Team moves the due date
→ Collection delayed for no reason

The requirement said:
"A national holiday anywhere stops an SDD collection."

Why?

SDD counting runs on Inter-PSP Business Days, defined as TARGET Business Days, so a national holiday elsewhere leaves the TARGET schedule and the collection validity untouched. TARGET drives Due Date, D-1 and settlement for the interbank journey, while each PSP applies its own Business Day calendar only to customer-facing service. Treating a national holiday calendar as the SDD Business Day calendar is the classic error, and the TARGET calendar is the one that controls the interbank leg.

TARGET governs the interbank leg. National holidays do not.

BA Takeaway

Use the TARGET calendar for the interbank leg, and each PSP's own calendar only for customer-facing service.

Keep these controls separate:

→ TARGET calendar
→ PSP calendar
→ Due Date

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves which calendar governs this collection?"

Have you moved a due date for a holiday that never applied?
takeaway: TARGET governs the interbank leg. National holidays do not.

parts.label: PSP calendar, customer service
parts.note: Each bank applies its own calendar to decide when customer service is open.

title: A EUR 50,000 payment went missing. The beneficiary could not prove it had been sent.
explain:
A EUR 50,000 payment is sent across borders.
The beneficiary says it never arrived.
The team searches by amount and date, and finds three matching payments.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 50,000 payment sent
→ Beneficiary says it never arrived
→ Team searches by amount and date
→ Three payments match, none can be proven

The requirement said:
"Amount and date are enough to trace a payment."

Why?

The UETR, the Unique End-to-End Transaction Reference, is a 36-character RFC 4122 identifier issued by the initiating bank and unchanged from originator to beneficiary. It lets a bank follow the journey from end to end, pinpoint where the payment sits at any moment, and carry the relevant details forward along the way, while also helping banks manage liquidity, exceptions and reconciliation. When the beneficiary thinks the money has not arrived, the UETR lets them claim, trace and prove the payment, which is why a payment lacking a UETR travels with no track at all.

One reference for the whole journey. Without it, there is no track.

BA Takeaway

Trace every payment by its UETR, unchanged from originator to beneficiary, and never by amount and date alone.

Keep these controls separate:

→ UETR
→ Payment journey
→ Claim and proof

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves which payment this is, end to end?"

Have you tried to trace a payment with only an amount and a date?
takeaway: One reference for the whole journey. Without it, there is no track.

parts.note: Assigned by the initiating bank, unchanged for the whole journey.

title: A EUR 40,000 payment crossed borders in 60 seconds. The beneficiary got exactly what was expected.
explain:
A EUR 40,000 cross-border payment is sent under OCT Inst.
Payment and settlement complete in 60 seconds.
The non-euro leg is converted before the beneficiary is paid, so the amount lands exactly as expected.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 40,000 OCT Inst payment sent
→ Payment and settlement in 60 seconds
→ Non-euro leg converted before payment
→ Beneficiary receives the expected amount

The requirement said:
"Speed is the test for a cross-border instant payment."

Why?

OCT Inst is already live and processes cross-border payments in 60 seconds, handling both the payment and the settlement, with both legs settled through the Euro system. The non-euro leg runs wholly outside the Euro area, governed by non-euro rules, standards and bank policies, with conversion completed before the beneficiary is paid, so the beneficiary receives exactly the amount expected. Speed is not the test here, reliability and rule-following are.

Speed is not the test. Reliability and rule-following are.

BA Takeaway

Judge every OCT Inst payment on whether the non-euro leg followed its rules and the beneficiary got the expected amount.

Keep these controls separate:

→ OCT Inst settlement
→ Non-euro leg rules
→ Beneficiary amount

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves the non-euro leg followed its rules?"

Have you judged a fast payment as a good payment?
takeaway: Speed is not the test. Reliability and rule-following are.

title: A EUR 25,000 payment left Europe for outside it. It cleared in 10 seconds, around the clock.
explain:
A EUR 25,000 payment starts in Europe and goes outside it.
The euro leg and the leg outside the euro area both have to work.
OCT Inst clears it in 10 seconds, and the team assumes the speed is the point.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 25,000 One-Leg Out payment sent
→ Euro leg plus non-euro leg
→ OCT Inst clears in 10 seconds
→ Team judges it on speed alone

The requirement said:
"One-Leg Out is a speed story."

Why?

One-Leg Out means a payment starts in Europe and goes outside it, with a euro leg plus a leg outside the euro area, and the One-Leg Out Instant Credit Transfer, OCT Inst, clears such cross-border payments in 10 seconds. As part of SEPA, OCT Inst follows the SEPA rule set, and clears and settles through the Euro leg, while payments can be made around the clock, every day of the year. Speed is not the point, an efficient, consistent and compliant process is.

Speed is not the point. An efficient, consistent and compliant process is.

BA Takeaway

Judge One-Leg Out on efficiency, consistency and compliance, with the 10 second clear as the result, not the goal.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Euro leg
→ Non-euro leg
→ SEPA rule set

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this payment was efficient, consistent and compliant?"

Have you called a 10 second payment a success without checking the process behind it?
takeaway: Speed is not the point. An efficient, consistent and compliant process is.

title: A EUR 500,000 payment on a blockchain network, and no one could say who settles it
explain:
A EUR 500,000 payment was sent across a blockchain payment network.

It arrived, but Operations could not say who had settled it or where the settlement proof sat.

The network had no single settlement account to point at.

Here's how it happened:

→ Payment sent between validated, keyed nodes
→ Every node holds a copy of the distributed ledger
→ Ledger refreshed with the transaction
→ Accounting posted to participant accounts inside the ledger
→ Settlement left to the network, with no central settlement account

The assumption was:
"Settlement works the same way as in a clearing system."

Why?

In a blockchain network there is no central bank account and no clearing house holding the settlement. Each participant maintains the ledger, and settlement is the ledger update itself. Compliance checks still have to run alongside near real time processing, and that is still a live discussion.

A shared ledger is not a settlement account.

BA Takeaway

Before routing a payment onto a new network, name the settlement proof, the account that holds it, and the control that runs beside the speed.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Node validation and keys
→ Ledger update as settlement
→ Participant accounts inside the ledger
→ Sanctions and compliance checks

The real requirement isn't "Can the network move the money fast?"

It's "What evidence proves the payment settled, and who holds that proof?"

Have you seen a new payment network where settlement proof was never named?
takeaway: A shared ledger is not a settlement account.

title: A EUR 2 million day settled in three moves, not two thousand
explain:
Two banks exchanged 2,000 payments in a day, worth EUR 2 million in total.

Under bilateral clearing they would have settled 2,000 separate positions.

Under multilateral clearing they settled just three net positions, and the day closed on time.

Here's how it happened:

→ 2,000 payments flow between banks during the day
→ Netting collapses them into a few positions
→ Each bank ends in one net debit or net credit
→ One connection to the clearing mechanism reaches every other bank
→ The mechanism manages credit risk for all participants

The assumption was:
"Every payment needs its own settlement."

Why?

Netting removes the need to settle each payment separately. Multilateral clearing dominates because it saves a huge number of transactions, and bilateral clearing stays rare, gaining appeal only where the banks involved are very large.

Netting turns thousands of payments into a handful of positions.

BA Takeaway

When a design proposes bilateral settlement, ask what netting would save and who carries the credit risk without a central mechanism.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Gross payment flows
→ Net positions after netting
→ Credit risk management
→ The single connection to the mechanism

The real requirement isn't "How do we settle each payment?"

It's "What evidence proves the net position is right and the risk is covered?"

Have you seen a design settle gross when netting would have done the job?
takeaway: Netting turns thousands of payments into a handful of positions.

title: EUR 4 million in net debits, and the settlement account was not a bank account
explain:
At the end of the clearing cycle, three banks owed a combined EUR 4 million in net debits.

Operations looked for the clearing mechanism's bank account to pay into.

There was none. The mechanism is a company, not a bank.

Here's how it happened:

→ Netting ends, each bank has a net debit or a net credit position
→ Net debit banks transfer funds to the mechanism
→ The mechanism settles through an account it holds with the central bank
→ The mechanism credits the accounts of banks in net credit positions
→ Settlement completes in central bank money

The assumption was:
"The clearing mechanism holds the money like a bank."

Why?

The mechanism is a company. It does not take deposits. It settles through its central bank account, so the funds move in central bank money with the mechanism in the middle.

The mechanism moves the money, it does not hold it.

BA Takeaway

When a design names a settlement account, check who owns it and what kind of money moves through it.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Net debit positions
→ Net credit positions
→ The central bank settlement account
→ The mechanism as intermediary, not holder

The real requirement isn't "Where do we send the settlement?"

It's "What evidence proves the funds moved in central bank money?"

Have you seen a settlement design assume the clearing mechanism was a bank?
takeaway: The mechanism moves the money, it does not hold it.

title: A EUR 50,000 payment arrived after cut-off, and the cycle had already closed
explain:
A EUR 50,000 payment was sent five minutes after the clearing cut-off.

The customer expected it in the same cycle.

It waited for the next one, because the cut-off had already fixed the cycle.

Here's how it happened:

→ Transactions flow to the mechanism from all banks
→ The mechanism tracks how many each bank sent and received
→ Cut-off arrives, no further transactions enter that cycle
→ Netting starts on what is available
→ Amounts in the messages let the mechanism compute each participant position
→ The late EUR 50,000 payment waits for the next cycle

The requirement said:
"Send the payment and it will settle today."

Why?

A cut-off is a hard time limit, not a guideline. Once it passes, netting runs on the transactions already in the cycle, and anything later is simply not in it.

Cut-off is a wall, not a suggestion.

BA Takeaway

Every payment design needs the cut-off named, the cycle it belongs to, and what happens to a payment that misses it.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Transaction flows into the cycle
→ The cut-off time
→ Netting on what is available
→ Positions computed from message amounts

The real requirement isn't "When was the payment sent?"

It's "What evidence proves which cycle the payment belongs to?"

Have you seen a customer promised same-cycle settlement after the cut-off passed?
takeaway: Cut-off is a wall, not a suggestion.

title: A pacs.008 worth EUR 120,000 failed validation, and no one could say which rule it broke
explain:
A pacs.008 worth EUR 120,000 failed validation.

The team argued for a day about which rule it had broken.

The answer was sitting in a free document nobody had opened.

Here's how it happened:

→ pacs.008 built and sent for validation
→ Validation fails, no rule cited
→ Team debates the message structure from memory
→ The Message Definition Report holds the content and the validation rules
→ The rule is found in the MDR and the message is fixed

The assumption was:
"Validation rules live in the team's heads."

Why?

Validation of a SWIFT MX message follows the ISO 20022 standard, and the authoritative place to read how a given message is validated is its Message Definition Report. The reports are free to download from the ISO 20022 website.

The MDR is the rulebook, not the team's memory.

BA Takeaway

When a message fails validation, go to the MDR first. Name the message, the rule, and the evidence before debating the fix.

Keep these controls separate:

→ The message as sent
→ The ISO 20022 standard
→ The MDR validation rules
→ The fix, applied to the right rule

The real requirement isn't "Why did validation fail?"

It's "What evidence in the MDR proves which rule was broken?"

Have you seen a validation failure debated for a day when the MDR had the answer?
takeaway: The MDR is the rulebook, not the team's memory.

title: A EUR 25,000 pacs.008 arrived, and the beneficiary waited until the next day
explain:
A EUR 25,000 pacs.008 arrived at the beneficiary bank on the settlement day.

The beneficiary was credited the next day.

The bank had kept a day of float it was never allowed to keep.

Here's how it happened:

→ pacs.008 arrives at the creditor agent
→ Settlement day arrives, funds available
→ Creditor agent holds the funds overnight
→ Beneficiary credited the next day
→ Customer complains, and the delay is found in the posting

The requirement said:
"Credit the beneficiary when the posting batch runs."

Why?

Once pacs.008 arrives, the creditor agent must put the funds at the beneficiary disposal on the settlement day. The Payment Services Directive leaves the beneficiary bank no float, so the credit cannot slip past that day. The settlement day itself is the maximum window.

The settlement day is the deadline, not the start of the window.

BA Takeaway

A credit deadline is a same-day obligation. If the posting batch runs the next day, the batch is wrong, not the rule.

Keep these controls separate:

→ pacs.008 arrival
→ Settlement day
→ Beneficiary credit
→ Float, which the bank is not allowed to keep

The real requirement isn't "When does the batch run?"

It's "What evidence proves the beneficiary was credited on the settlement day?"

Have you seen a beneficiary credited late because the batch ran the next day?
takeaway: The settlement day is the deadline, not the start of the window.

title: One MT101 for EUR 60,000 in payables, and the ERP only spoke one language
explain:
A corporate had EUR 60,000 in payables to send: domestic transfers, a cheque payment, and a cross-border payment.

Its ERP generated one MT101.

Every payment went out on the same message, because the ERP only had to speak one language.

Here's how it happened:

→ Corporate ERP generates one MT101 for all payables
→ Domestic RTGS, EFT and ACH payments start on MT101
→ Cheque payments start on MT101
→ Cross-border payments start on MT101
→ One standard format covers every kind of payment the corporate makes

The assumption was:
"MT101 is only for cross-border payments."

Why?

Corporates initiate domestic payments with MT101 just as they initiate cross-border ones. The commercial logic is simple: one standard format from the ERP initiates all payables, so the corporate does not maintain a different format per payment type.

One format from the ERP, every payable covered.

BA Takeaway

When a corporate asks for a new payment type, check first whether the MT101 it already sends can carry it, before building a second channel.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Domestic payments on MT101
→ Cross-border payments on MT101
→ The single ERP format
→ Each payment type it initiates

The real requirement isn't "Which message starts this payment?"

It's "What evidence proves the existing MT101 flow already covers it?"

Have you seen a second payment channel built when the MT101 already did the job?
takeaway: One format from the ERP, every payable covered.

title: A EUR 90,000 MT101 arrived at the concentrating bank, and the bank passed it on untouched
explain:
A corporate sent one MT101 worth EUR 90,000 to its concentrating bank, covering three destination banks.

The concentrating bank did not write three new instructions.

It forwarded the same MT101, split per destination, and processed only its own share.

Here's how it happened:

→ Corporate sends one MT101 to the concentrating bank
→ Concentrating bank receives the MT101
→ Same MT101 forwarded to each destination bank
→ The bank extracts the MT101 due to each destination
→ It processes its own instruction, the one where it stands as debtor bank

The assumption was:
"Each bank in the chain writes a new instruction."

Why?

In the concentration cases the bank forwards the MT101 it received instead of originating a new one. The same instruction travels onward, split per destination where needed, so nothing is re-keyed and nothing drifts from the original.

Forward the instruction, do not rewrite it.

BA Takeaway

When a payment passes through a concentrating bank, check that the original instruction survives intact and that each destination gets its own extract.

Keep these controls separate:

→ The MT101 as received
→ The MT101 as forwarded per destination
→ The bank's own instruction as debtor bank
→ The original instruction, unchanged

The real requirement isn't "Did we create the onward instructions?"

It's "What evidence proves the forwarded MT101 matches the original?"

Have you seen a payment re-keyed in the middle of a chain and changed by it?
takeaway: Forward the instruction, do not rewrite it.

title: A EUR 15,000 SEPA payment on an MT101, and the bank said it could not carry it
explain:
A corporate sent a EUR 15,000 SEPA payment on an MT101.

One bank processed it. Another refused it.

Both were right, because whether a bank processes MT101 as a SEPA payment turns entirely on that bank's own capabilities.

Here's how it happened:

→ Corporate sends a SEPA payment on MT101
→ Bank A processes it as SEPA
→ Bank B refuses it, the message cannot hold all the information
→ The missing information is what pain.001 can carry and MT101 cannot

The assumption was:
"If MT101 can carry SEPA, every bank will process it."

Why?

A SEPA payment can travel on an MT101, but the message cannot hold all the information a pain.001 can carry. Where the information fits, MT101 works for SEPA. Where it does not, pain.001 is the right message.

MT101 can carry SEPA, but only as far as the information fits.

BA Takeaway

Before choosing the message, check what information the payment needs and whether the receiving bank can process it. The message choice follows the data, not the habit.

Keep these controls separate:

→ The information the payment needs
→ What MT101 can carry
→ What pain.001 can carry
→ The receiving bank's capability

The real requirement isn't "Can MT101 carry SEPA?"

It's "What evidence proves the receiving bank can process this payment on MT101?"

Have you seen a payment refused because the message could not carry the data?
takeaway: MT101 can carry SEPA, but only as far as the information fits.

title: An MT101 for EUR 40,000 arrived, and the debit and the money took different messages
explain:
A corporate sent an MT101 for EUR 40,000 to its bank.

The account was debited, but no money moved.

The MT101 only instructs the debit. The money moves on a different message.

Here's how it happened:

→ Corporate sends MT101 to the bank
→ Account servicing institution holds the account to be debited
→ ASI processes the MT101 against that account
→ ASI issues an MT103 to move the funds onward
→ The MT101 instructs the debit and the MT103 carries the money

The assumption was:
"The MT101 moves the money."

Why?

The account servicing institution is the bank holding the account to be debited. On receiving the MT101 it processes the instruction against that account, then it issues an MT103 to move the funds onward. Two messages, two jobs.

MT101 instructs, MT103 carries.

BA Takeaway

When a payment stalls after the debit, check whether the onward MT103 was ever issued. The debit is not the payment.

Keep these controls separate:

→ The MT101 instruction
→ The account debit
→ The MT103 onward movement
→ The funds arriving at the beneficiary

The real requirement isn't "Was the account debited?"

It's "What evidence proves the MT103 was issued and the funds moved?"

Have you seen a payment treated as done because the debit posted?
takeaway: MT101 instructs, MT103 carries.

title: A EUR 3,000 direct debit arrived with no mandate, and the creditor bank paid it anyway
explain:
A pacs.003 direct debit for EUR 3,000 arrived at the creditor bank.

There was no active mandate behind it.

The bank processed it anyway, because the scheme does not require it to check.

Here's how it happened:

→ Creditor sends pacs.003 for EUR 3,000
→ Creditor bank receives the collection
→ No mandate check is run
→ Collection processed, debtor account debited
→ Debtor disputes the collection afterwards

The assumption was:
"The creditor bank must check the mandate."

Why?

SEPA applies the creditor driven mandate flow, so the creditor bank carries no obligation to check a pacs.003 against an active mandate. The creditor bank may still validate if it chooses, but the scheme does not require it. That contrasts with a debtor driven flow, where the debtor side holds the mandate.

No obligation to check does not mean no risk.

BA Takeaway

When a design relies on a mandate check, name who owns it. If the creditor bank does not own it, the control must live somewhere else, or the dispute will.

Keep these controls separate:

→ The pacs.003 collection
→ The mandate, held on the creditor side
→ The optional validation
→ The dispute when the mandate is missing

The real requirement isn't "Did we check the mandate?"

It's "What evidence proves someone owns the mandate check?"

Have you seen a direct debit collected with no mandate behind it?
takeaway: No obligation to check does not mean no risk.

title: A store voucher for R1,000 shoes worked, and the customer asked why it could not pay anywhere
explain:
A customer bought shoes worth R1,000 with a clothing store voucher.

It worked perfectly in that store.

Then the customer tried to use the same voucher at a shop across the road, and it was refused.

Here's how it happened:

→ Customer pays R1,000 with a store voucher
→ Voucher accepted at the issuing store
→ Customer tries the voucher at another shop
→ Voucher refused, it only works inside its own loop
→ Customer asks why a payment that worked once cannot work everywhere

The assumption was:
"A payment that works is a payment that works everywhere."

Why?

The voucher is a closed loop system, usually run by a non-financial service provider, and the payment is used for goods or services inside that loop only. An open loop system is run by financial service providers regulated within the national payment system, and its payments work across the system.

A closed loop payment works inside its loop, and only there.

BA Takeaway

When a payment product is designed, name the loop first. The loop decides where the payment works, who regulates it, and what the customer can expect.

Keep these controls separate:

→ The closed loop and its issuer
→ The open loop and its regulated providers
→ Where the payment is accepted
→ What the customer was told

The real requirement isn't "Can the customer pay?"

It's "What evidence proves the customer knows where this payment works?"

Have you seen a customer caught out by a payment that only worked in one place?
takeaway: A closed loop payment works inside its loop, and only there.

title: A customer tried to pay EUR 10,000 with a promissory note, and the bank said no
explain:
A customer walked into a bank with a promissory note for EUR 10,000 and asked to pay with it.

The law in that country allowed private individuals to issue one.

The bank refused it anyway.

Here's how it happened:

→ Customer offers a personal promissory note for EUR 10,000
→ In some countries, such as France, only businesses can issue promissory notes
→ In this country the law permits private individuals to issue them
→ The bank stays silent about them and steers people toward bank loans
→ The bank refuses the note, even where the law allows it

The assumption was:
"If the law allows it, the bank must accept it."

Why?

Legal permission is not the same as bank acceptance. Banks stay silent about promissory notes and steer people toward bank loans, which are legally and financially more interesting for the banks. A bank or finance company may therefore refuse a personal promissory note even where the law allows it.

Legal does not mean accepted.

BA Takeaway

When a payment instrument is designed, check three gates separately: the law, the bank's policy, and the customer's understanding. All three must pass.

Keep these controls separate:

→ What the law permits
→ What the bank accepts
→ What the customer is told
→ The alternative the bank offers instead

The real requirement isn't "Is this instrument legal?"

It's "What evidence proves the bank will accept it?"

Have you seen a legal payment method refused at the counter?
takeaway: Legal does not mean accepted.

title: A EUR 2,000 card payment through a wallet arrived in seconds, but the bank account was debited two days later
explain:
A customer paid EUR 2,000 by card through a wallet.

The seller was credited right away.

The customer's bank account was debited two days later, and the customer thought the money had been taken twice.

Here's how it happened:

→ Customer pays EUR 2,000 by card through the wallet
→ Wallet checks the balance and credits the beneficiary at once
→ Bank account behind the card is debited one or two days later
→ Customer sees the credit and the late debit and reports a double charge
→ Investigation shows one payment, two timings

The assumption was:
"Push and pull describe the technology."

Why?

Push and pull describe the movement of the instruction and the funds, never the technology behind the payment. A credit transfer started directly from a bank account counts as push, with the account debited right away. A PayPal reserve debit sent straight to the beneficiary counts as push. Paying by card through the wallet counts as pull, and the timing gap is built into it.

The same payment can look instant and delayed at the same time.

BA Takeaway

When a payment journey mixes push and pull, show the customer both timings. The debit timing and the credit timing are separate facts.

Keep these controls separate:

→ The instruction and the funds movement
→ The beneficiary credit timing
→ The bank account debit timing
→ The customer's view of both

The real requirement isn't "Did the payment go through?"

It's "What evidence proves the customer can see when each leg moves?"

Have you seen a customer report a double charge that was really one pull payment?
takeaway: The same payment can look instant and delayed at the same time.

explain:
A customer tried to move EUR 5,000 from a mobile wallet to a bank account.

The transfer failed for insufficient funds.

The customer had EUR 5,000 in the bank account, and assumed that was enough.

Here's how it happened:

→ Customer moves EUR 5,000 from wallet to bank
→ Wallet holds only EUR 1,200
→ Transfer refused, wallet has insufficient funds
→ Customer complains, pointing at the bank balance
→ The bank balance is irrelevant, the wallet is the source account

The assumption was:
"My money is my money, whichever account it sits in."

Why?

Moving funds between a mobile wallet and a bank account means moving money between two accounts belonging to the same customer, and push transactions should be enough for these moves. But a wallet to bank transfer should start only when the wallet holds sufficient funds, and a bank to wallet transfer only when the bank account holds sufficient funds. The source account is the one that must be funded.

Same owner, different accounts, different balances.

BA Takeaway

When a transfer moves money between a customer's own accounts, the funds check must run on the source account, and the error must say which account is short.

Keep these controls separate:

→ The wallet balance
→ The bank account balance
→ The source account funds check
→ The error message naming the short account

The real requirement isn't "Does the customer have the money?"

It's "What evidence proves the source account holds the funds?"

Have you seen a transfer refused when the customer clearly had the money, in the other account?
